title: Energy-Efficiency Rebates
summary: VERIFY → OPEN PROGRAMS → ORDER → PROTECT YOUR TITLE
subtitle: A clipboard is not proof of anything. Only your own phone call is.

blocks.text: The man at the door has a clipboard and a lanyard. He is friendly, he knows your street, and he says a government rebate program by name. None of that is proof of anything.
Natural Resources Canada does not send anyone to your door. It says so on its own website.

Energy rebates changed twice in the last two years, and most of what you find online is out of date. This module sorts out what is open right now, the order that keeps a claim valid, the true cost of waiting for a rebate, and how to keep a salesperson from ending up on your property title.
Knowing what is open today, and in what order to act, protects both your rebate and your home.
blocks.detail: The old federal grants closed, new programs replaced them, and the order of steps decides whether you get paid.
blocks.extra: Section 02 sorts what is open from what is closed.

sections.title: What Is Open, What Is Closed

blocks.text: Most of what you find when you search this topic is confidently out of date. Here is where things stand.

items.title: Closed
list: Canada Greener Homes Grant: stopped taking applicants in February 2024. Its last paperwork deadline was December 31, 2025
Canada Greener Homes Loan: the last day to apply was October 1, 2025
Both still show up everywhere online as though you can apply tomorrow. You cannot

items.title: Open
list: Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program: free installed upgrades for low- to middle-income homeowners and tenants, only where your province has signed on
Oil to Heat Pump Affordability: still the largest single incentive for a home heated with oil
Provincial and utility programs, which for many households are now the main event

blocks.text: It is tempting to read “the grant closed” and assume the money is gone. It moved. The federal dollars shifted from a broad reimbursement anyone could claim toward a targeted, no-cost install for lower-income households, delivered by the provinces. At the same time, provincial programs got substantially bigger. Start with your provincial program page and your utility, not with a federal search, and ignore any article about this topic that is more than six months old.

items.title: When one grant closes, the money often moves somewhere else.

items.title: “The government sent someone to my door about the rebate.”
items.text: It did not. No federal energy program uses unsolicited door-to-door or phone contact, and NRCan says so plainly. If someone arrives uninvited, take the company name, close the door, and look the program up yourself. Nothing legitimate is lost by waiting a day.

blocks.text: Canada: Canada Greener Homes Initiative
These programs change names and terms too often for a printed list to stay honest for long. Start with the operator, not the program name.

items.title: Ontario
items.text: Home Renovation Savings Program, delivered by Save on Energy and Enbridge Gas. Single-upgrade and bundled paths. Condos, apartments and new builds are excluded.

items.title: British Columbia
items.text: CleanBC Better Homes, with an income-qualified tier that pays substantially more. BC Hydro rebates stack on top.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Rénoclimat for the building envelope, Hydro-Québec’s LogisVert for equipment, and Chauffez vert for getting off oil.

items.title: Manitoba
items.text: Efficiency Manitoba, and the first province delivering the federal affordability program.

items.title: Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
items.text: Efficiency Nova Scotia and NB Power’s Total Home Energy Savings Program. Nova Scotia’s heat pump support is among the most generous in the country.

items.title: Alberta and Saskatchewan
items.text: Thinner coverage. Check SaskPower’s retrofit rebate and your municipality.

items.title: Municipal
items.text: Several cities run their own low-interest retrofit loan programs, repaid through the property tax bill.

items.title: “There is a thirty percent federal tax credit for home solar.”
items.text: There is a thirty percent Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit. It is for taxable Canadian corporations, not for people putting panels on their own roof. This one circulates constantly in homeowner forums. Read who is allowed to claim it before you build a budget on it.

blocks.text: Almost every rejected rebate fails for the same reason: the homeowner did the work first and applied afterward. If your program needs an assessment, it needs it before anything is touched. There is no appeal for a furnace that is already installed.

items.title: Find out which path your program uses
items.text: Most provinces now offer two. A single-upgrade path, where you install one thing with no assessment required. And a bundled path, combining insulation, air sealing and windows for a larger total, but only after a pre-retrofit assessment.

items.title: Book the pre-retrofit evaluation, if your path needs one
items.text: You book it. A registered energy advisor does it. The report shows where your home leaks and which upgrades qualify.

items.title: Confirm what stacks before you choose equipment
items.text: Federal, provincial and utility rebates can often be combined on the same upgrade. Each one has its own list of approved equipment.

items.title: Use a contractor from the program’s list
items.text: Most programs require registered or certified installers. A cheaper quote from someone off the list is not cheaper.

items.title: Do the work, keep every invoice and model number
items.text: Programs verify specific equipment, not general descriptions.

items.title: Complete the post-retrofit evaluation and submit on time
items.text: This second evaluation is what proves the improvement, and its deadline is a real one.

blocks.text: Quick math: is the bundle worth it?

Add up the cost of the two evaluations, minus whatever the program rebates back for them. Compare the total bundled rebate against the total single-upgrade rebate for the same work. Then price the weeks of delay: another winter on a dying furnace is a real cost, not a rounding error. If the bundled premium clearly beats the evaluation cost, take the bundle. If it is close and your furnace is limping, take the single upgrade and stop optimizing.

items.title: “I will start the work now and apply once it is finished.”
items.text: This is the most expensive sentence in the module. On any bundled or assessment-based path, work started before the pre-retrofit evaluation disqualifies the whole claim. If a contractor tells you it will be fine, ask them to put that in writing next to their name.

sections.title: The Gap Between Invoice and Rebate

blocks.text: A rebate is not a discount. With most programs, you pay the contractor in full and then wait, often several months, for a cheque. The exception is the federal affordability program. There, the program pays the contractor and the household pays nothing.

That gap is where energy retrofits quietly turn into credit problems. Putting a heat pump on a high-rate credit card while waiting for a rebate can erase most of the rebate, and every month of delay costs more. A rebate you have not received yet is not money you have. Check whether your province or city offers low-interest or on-bill financing, ask the program whether it pays the contractor directly, or phase the work so each piece is paid from cash rather than credit.

Then run the real math. Here are three ways to pay for the same $10,000 heat pump: a 0% program or city loan over 40 months, a bank loan at about 8% over five years, and contractor financing at about 15% over five years. Compare what each costs to borrow, then set that against the rebate you are waiting for.
Price the wait for your rebate
blocks.extra: Enter the amount you need, then each offer’s monthly payment and number of payments. Watch the borrowing cost update.

blocks.text: In this example, contractor financing costs about $4,280 to borrow, while the bank loan costs about $2,180 and the 0% loan costs nothing. If your rebate is $5,000, the most expensive option eats most of it. When the borrowing cost is a big share of the rebate, the timing is wrong, not the project.

items.title: “The rebate will pay off the loan, so the interest does not matter.”
items.text: The interest is charged while you wait, and it is not refunded. A slow rebate on an expensive loan can leave you paying for months after the cheque arrives.

blocks.text: For years, door-to-door sales of home equipment in Ontario followed a pattern. A salesperson who showed up uninvited would set up a rental or financing deal for a water heater or furnace. Then they would register a notice of security interest against the title of the home. Many owners only found out when they tried to sell.

Ontario’s Homeowner Protection Act, in force since June 2024, banned new NOSIs for consumer goods and deemed existing ones expired. They can be removed from title on application, for a government fee. Other provinces have not all followed. If you own a home in Ontario and ever signed an equipment agreement at your door, a title search is worth doing. In any province, before signing anything for home equipment, ask directly whether anything will be registered against your title, and get the answer in writing.
Six checks before you sign for home equipment

items.title: You called
items.text: You contacted them, not the other way around.

items.title: Real program
items.text: The program is named on a provincial, federal or utility website, not just a brochure.

items.title: On the list
items.text: The contractor is on the program’s registered installer list.

items.title: Title in writing
items.text: You asked in writing whether anything will be registered against your property title.

items.title: Way out
items.text: You have read what happens if you cancel, and when that window closes.

items.title: No rush
items.text: Nobody has told you the offer expires today.

sections.title: Priya, the Lanyard and the Twenty Minutes That Settled It

blocks.text: Priya and the lanyard
paragraphs: Priya lives in Brampton with her husband and his father. The furnace is twenty-two years old and loud. Her goal is to replace it before next winter without going into debt.
One morning in March, a man knocks. He has a lanyard, a tablet and the name of a federal program Priya has read about. He wants to check the furnace now, because the funding is almost gone.
Her father-in-law answers the door, because he is retired and considers it his job. He is polite and lets the man talk. The man says they can sign today and lock in the rebate.

Priya feels the pull. The furnace is old, and the man seems to know the program. She makes a choice. She asks for a business card and says they will call back. It is a sentence with no downside, and it is far harder to say than it looks when someone helpful is standing in your doorway.

That evening, she spends twenty minutes on the Natural Resources Canada site. She finds a notice in plain words: no outside company is allowed to contact you about the program, and only homeowners book the home check. She also learns the grant he half-named closed the year before, and Ontario has not signed on to the program that replaced it.

The twist is good news. Ontario’s own program has a single-upgrade path that needs no home check at all. Priya picks a contractor from the program’s list and replaces the furnace with a cold-climate heat pump.
The rebate arrives that summer. The man with the lanyard never calls back, which tells them everything they need to know about how badly he wanted the work.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Can you still apply for the Canada Greener Homes Grant or Loan?
items.detail: No. The grant stopped taking applicants in February 2024, and the loan’s last application day was October 1, 2025.

items.title: Who pays the contractor in the federal affordability program?
items.detail: The program does. Eligible households pay nothing for the installed upgrades.

items.title: You start the work, then book the home check. What happens on a bundled path?
items.detail: The claim is usually disqualified. The pre-retrofit evaluation must come before any work.

items.title: A $10,000 loan is paid at $238 a month for 60 months. What does it cost to borrow?
items.detail: About $4,280. That is $238 × 60 = $14,280, minus the $10,000 borrowed.

items.title: Someone knocks and says the rebate funding runs out today. What do you do?
items.detail: Take a business card, close the door and look the program up yourself. NRCan does not send anyone to your door.

items.title: What should you ask before signing for home equipment in any province?
items.detail: Whether anything will be registered against your property title, with the answer in writing.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Retrofit Plan

blocks.text: This week: open your provincial program page and your utility’s rebate page, and write today’s date next to what you find. Undated notes go stale in months. Find the exact sentence about when work may begin and copy it out. If you heat with oil, check the Oil to Heat Pump Affordability program before anything else. If you cannot find the start-work rule in the program’s own words, phone them.
Everything real in this module starts with you picking up the phone.
blocks.detail: Check what is open this month, not what a blog says. Start with your province and your utility, not Ottawa. Finish the home check before anyone touches the house, price the wait for your rebate, and never sign for home equipment without asking, in writing, what gets registered against your title.

items.title: EnerGuide evaluation
items.text: A home energy assessment by a registered energy advisor. It produces a rating and a list of qualifying upgrades. Booked by the homeowner, never sold at the door.

items.title: Registered energy advisor
items.text: The certified expert who does the home check, working through a licensed company.

items.title: CGHAP
items.text: Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program. Free federal home upgrades for households with low to middle incomes and tenants, run by provinces that signed on.

items.title: OHPA
items.text: Oil to Heat Pump Affordability. Federal help for homes switching off oil heat, often topped up by the province.

items.title: Stacking
items.text: Combining federal, provincial, utility and city rebates on the same upgrade, where each program allows it.

items.title: Single-upgrade vs bundled path
items.text: One upgrade with no home check, compared with several upgrades that need a home check before and after and pay more in total.

items.title: Cold-climate heat pump
items.text: A heat pump rated to keep working at low outdoor temperatures. The rating, not the label, is what programs check.

items.title: NOSI
items.text: Notice of security interest. A note on a property title tied to equipment you financed or rented. Banned for consumer goods in Ontario since June 2024. Rules differ elsewhere.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Natural Resources Canada: the authoritative page for federal programs and current energy-scam warnings.
Your provincial program or utility: Save on Energy, CleanBC Better Homes, Rénoclimat and LogisVert, Efficiency Manitoba, Efficiency Nova Scotia, NB Power, SaskPower.
Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: 1-888-495-8501, to report a door-to-door or telephone approach.
Provincial consumer protection office: for cancelling a contract signed under pressure. Cancellation windows are short, act the same week.
A community legal clinic or real estate lawyer: if something has already been registered against your title.

blocks.text: This module skips rebate amounts on purpose. Rebate levels, income thresholds and equipment lists in this field change several times a year. The loan example is for practice only. Confirm every figure on the program’s own page the day you need it.
